lakeHero.audience: For disaster teams in Gilgit-Baltistan and upper Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
lakeHero.title: Glacial lakes through the clouds, seen by radar
lakeHero.lede: This shows how often NISAR radar looked at each glacial lake while clouds blocked optical satellites, and whether the radar water area moved beyond its own noise.
lakeHero.screening: Indicative screening on provisional NISAR data; official warnings come from PMD, NDMA, GBDMA and PDMA.
lakeHero.headlineSource: Valid looks are NISAR passes that passed the checks on How we know. Provisional data.

beats.label: The cloud gap
beats.title: Clouds hid the lakes after 16 June

quote.text: Persistent cloud cover after 16 June 2026 has limited the availability of cloud-free satellite imagery, making it difficult to accurately assess lake area changes during the last three to four days.

body: NISAR is a radar satellite, so cloud does not stop it. Between {cloud_start} and {cloud_end} it made {cloud_looks} valid looks across {cloud_lakes} of the {lake_count} lakes on this list.
A valid look is one pass that passed our checks. It is not a measure of change: Lake Watch gives that lake by lake, with the date, the look count and the noise.
noData: NISAR is a radar satellite, so cloud does not stop it. Lake data is not in this build, so no counts are shown here.

beats.label: How radar sees lakes
beats.title: Calm water is dark, and shadow is dark from one side only
body: Calm water acts like a mirror for radar. The beam bounces away from the satellite, so little comes back and the lake looks dark.
Steep mountains can look dark too. Where a slope faces away from the satellite, the radar cannot see the ground behind the ridge, and that radar shadow is dark.

NISAR looks at the same ground from two directions on different passes, ascending and descending. A shadow falls on a different side of a ridge from each direction, but water stays dark from both. So we first mark shadow-prone pixels: dark in one direction's season median image and seen, not dark, in the other's. Then, in each pass, a dark pixel inside the lake zone counts as water unless it is shadow-prone.
The cost is that a lake whose shore lies in shadow loses some of its area in our count. How we know gives the thresholds.

beats.label: Lake Watch
beats.title: Lake Watch: one status for each lake
body: Lake Watch lists {watch_list}, each with a status: Growing, Stable, Shrinking, Change not confirmed yet, Frozen (likely), Frozen (seen by Sentinel-2), Break-up likely, Not seen this pass, Not observable, Not enough NISAR looks yet, or No lake now.

Frozen (likely) comes from air temperature at the lake, and Frozen (seen by Sentinel-2) from a clear optical image. Radar cannot tell new ice from open water, and frozen ground around a lake can read as water, so a frozen lake gets no growing or shrinking verdict until it thaws.

No lake now marks a site where recent imagery shows no lake, such as the empty basin of an ice-dammed lake that has drained. It gets no growing or shrinking verdict, and its dark radar area is not counted as lake area; the site stays on the list to watch for a lake forming.

A status compares a lake only with its own earlier passes from the same track. Growing or Shrinking needs a change larger than {change_factor} times the lake's own noise, so a label can change between passes on a small change.
Control lakes, kept to check the method, are listed last.
noData: Lake data is not in this build. Lake Watch lists each lake with a status once data/lakes.json is present.

beats.label: Limits and next steps
beats.title: What this does not tell you, and what comes next
body: This is indicative screening on provisional NISAR data. Official warnings come from PMD, NDMA, GBDMA and PDMA.

A status compares a lake only with its own earlier passes. Areas count water inside each lake's outline or search circle, and underestimate lakes whose shores sit in radar shadow. Frozen lakes, lakes under 0.05 km² and wind-roughened water are not validated. In the Sentinel-2 cross-check, radar water {optical_overlap}, one date per lake. So it is not a validation of lake extent.

Next steps to agree with the administration: SUPARCO's lake IDs and locations, so areas can be compared; which lakes district teams most need on the list; ground reports from those teams; and a re-run when NASA reprocesses the files.
